title: The path with the smallest maximum
sub: Path With Minimum Effort and Swim in Rising Water: Dijkstra with max, binary search on the answer, Union-Find in increasing order — and how to choose
cards/0/title: The problem: a route costs as much as its worst step
cards/0/body:
Path With Minimum Effort (LeetCode #1631). A height map heights of rows × cols, both up to 100, heights from 1 to 10⁶. Walk from the top-left corner to the bottom-right one in 4 directions. The effort of a route is the largest height difference between neighbouring cells on it. Find the smallest effort.

The cost here is not a sum but a maximum: a long gentle route beats a short one with a single wall. The signals of this pattern are "minimise the worst":

1. The cost of a path is its steepest step, its highest cell, its most dangerous spot.
2. The mirror version is "maximise the worst": the weakest bridge on the route should carry as much load as possible.
3. Neither the number of steps nor the sum matters.

In a game: "what is the smallest jump height a character needs to finish the level"; checking that a procedural level is traversable. A NavMesh agent has Step Height and Max Slope — fixed thresholds; and the question "what is the smallest Step Height this map needs" is exactly #1631.
cards/1/q: In which problems is the cost of a path its worst step rather than a sum? Select all that apply.
cards/1/options/0: The smallest jump height a character needs to hop across platforms to the exit
cards/1/options/1: Water rises one unit per second; when can you swim from corner to corner if you may only swim over flooded cells
cards/1/options/2: The heaviest load you can haul from A to B when every bridge has its own limit
cards/1/options/3: The smallest total travel time over roads of different lengths
cards/1/options/4: The fewest steps from the entrance to the exit of a maze
cards/1/explain: The jump is decided by the highest ledge on the path, the water by the highest cell, the load by the weakest bridge (the mirror: a maximum of minimums). Total travel time is ordinary Dijkstra over sums; the number of steps is BFS.
cards/2/title: Solution 1: Dijkstra with max instead of a sum
cards/2/body:
Enumerating routes is exponential, and BFS counts steps, not height differences. Dijkstra fits, though — what it needs is not a sum but one property: the cost of a path does not decrease when the path is extended. Here max(e, |Δh|) ≥ e, just like a weight ≥ 0 in a sum. So the cell with the smallest known effort is already final, and everything from the previous lesson works: lazy deletion, "popped means final".

What changes: effort[y, x] is the best known effort, and relaxation is max(e, |h[y][x] − h[r][c]|). And since a popped cell is final, you can stop as soon as the goal comes out of the heap, without draining the queue.

Cost: V = rows·cols ≤ 10⁴, about 4V edges. O(E log V) ≈ 4·10⁴ · 14 ≈ 6·10⁵ — plenty of headroom.
cards/3/q: Assemble Dijkstra for Path With Minimum Effort.
cards/3/explain: The goal is popped, so its effort e is final — return it. The cost of a step to a neighbour is the maximum of the path effort and the height difference, not their sum: a sum would count the whole climb, while we need the steepest step. Improve only when it got strictly better.
cards/4/task: Step through Dijkstra with max on a 3 × 4 map. The small number in a cell corner is its current effort. The rig stops twice: on a relaxation and at the moment the goal leaves the queue.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: max(1, 1) = 1 — better than 2: (1, 1) gets effort 1, and 1:(1, 1) is queued
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Nothing: (1, 1) is already in the queue
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: We pop (1, 2) with effort 1, height 6. Its neighbour (1, 1) has height 7 and effort 2 right now (reached from (0, 1) over a difference of 2). What happens to (1, 1)?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: The difference is 7 − 6 = 1, and the path cost is max(1, 1) = 1 < 2: the path through (1, 2) is better, even though it is longer. A new entry 1:(1, 1) is queued, and the old 2:(1, 1) will later surface as stale — you can see it further on in the rig.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: return 2: the goal is popped, its effort is final
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: Check the goal's neighbours in case a path with less effort exists
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: Drain the queue and return the minimum
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: The bottom-right cell, 2:(2, 3), is first in the queue. What does the code do when it pops it?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: Everything left in the queue is at least 2, and extending a path never lowers its cost. So no route to the goal can beat 2: popped means final. The remaining 4:(0, 3), 4:(2, 0) and the rest are never needed.
cards/5/q: On heights = [[1, 2], [4, 6]] this code returns 4, but the answer is 3. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/5/explain: The code returns when the goal first gets an estimate, not when it leaves the heap. Cell (0, 1) is popped first with effort 1, and from it the difference to the goal is |6 − 2| = 4 — the code returns 4 at once. Through (1, 0) the path costs max(3, |6 − 4|) = 3. An estimate is final only when it leaves the heap: check for the goal right after TryDequeue.
cards/6/title: Solution 2: binary search on the answer and BFS
cards/6/body:
Rephrase it: "can I get through if every step is at most X?" That is a plain BFS that refuses height differences above X: O(V + E). The check is monotone: if you get through with X, you get through with anything larger. So the answer is the smallest X for which it is true, and the template from the lesson on searching the answer finds it.

Bounds: the effort is at least 0 and at most 10⁶ − 1, the largest possible difference. That is about 20 checks of ≈ 5·10⁴ operations each: ≈ 10⁶ in total. No heap at all.

Unity: the same check — "is the map traversable for a character with jump X" — is useful on its own too, when a procedural generator rejects levels.
cards/7/body:
Union-Find (disjoint sets; covered in depth in the last lesson of the unit on graphs) stores groups as trees in a parent array: a root has parent[x] == x, and the root names the group. Find(x) climbs to the root and compresses the path on the way, hanging every visited node straight onto the root. Union(a, b) finds both roots and puts one under the other by rank: the shorter tree goes under the taller one, and the rank (a bound on height) grows only on a tie. Together this is almost O(1) per operation. a and b are in one group ⇔ Find(a) == Find(b).

The idea. Add edges from cheap to expensive and after each one ask: are the corners connected yet? The weight of the edge that connects them is the answer: before it only cheaper edges were available, and the corners were apart.

Swim in Rising Water (LeetCode #778, hard). An n × n grid, n ≤ 50, with heights that are all the numbers 0..n² − 1, each exactly once. At time t the water level is t; you can swim between neighbours if both cells are at most t high, and swimming takes no time. When can you get from (0, 0) to (n − 1, n − 1)? It is the same minimax: the answer is the highest cell on the best route. The heights are a permutation, so no sort is needed: at time t exactly cell cellAt[t] gets wet. For #1631 the neighbour edges are sorted by height difference: O(E log E).
cards/8/task: Step through Swim in Rising Water on a 4 × 4 grid: S is at height 0, E at height 5. Each step is a new water level and one newly wet cell. The rig asks twice what Union-Find will do.
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: E becomes a new separate pool
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: E merges two pools into one
cards/8/goal/asks/0/q: t = 5: E (3, 3) gets wet. Next to it, (3, 2) at height 3 and (2, 3) at height 4 are already wet, each on its own. What happens?
cards/8/goal/asks/0/explain: E touches two different groups, and two Union calls merge them into one. But Find(0) ≠ Find(15): S's group is the top-left corner, and E is not connected to it. No answer yet; the water keeps rising.
cards/8/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: S's pool grows, E is still apart
cards/8/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: The pools of S and E merge — the answer is 9
cards/8/goal/asks/1/q: t = 9: (2, 1) gets wet. Above it is (1, 1) from S's pool; to the right, (2, 2), and below, (3, 1), both from E's pool. What happens?
cards/8/goal/asks/1/explain: The cell touches both groups, and Union merges them: now Find(0) == Find(15), and the function returns 9. That is the minimax: on the best route S → (0, 1) → (1, 1) → (2, 1) → (3, 1) → (3, 2) → E the highest cell is 9.
cards/9/title: How to choose, and what to tell the interviewer
cards/9/body:
Three solutions to one problem is a strong move in an interview: name all three with their cost, pick one and say why.

Dijkstra with max — O(E log V). The default: works with any weights, fractional ones included, and stops as soon as the goal is popped.
Binary search + BFS — O((V + E) log W), where W is the range of the answer. The simplest code and no heap at all, but it needs an integer range that is not too wide. For fractional weights you search not over values but over the sorted list of differences.
Union-Find in increasing order — a sort in O(E log E) plus almost O(1) per edge. Best when no sort is needed, as in #778, and when you need answers for many thresholds at once: one sort and one pass serve all the queries, if they are known in advance.

What to say: "the path cost is a maximum, and it never decreases when the path is extended, so Dijkstra is correct; the alternative is binary search on the answer with BFS, because the check is monotone".
cards/9/code:
// Swim in Rising Water with the same Dijkstra: a cell costs max(path time, its height)
int cost = Math.Max(t, grid[y][x]);
cards/9/deep:
The link to spanning trees. A path with the smallest maximum between any two vertices can be taken along a minimum spanning tree: the cut property says the lightest edge across any cut belongs to the tree, so the bottleneck of the tree path is no worse than that of any other path. Union-Find in increasing order is Kruskal stopped at the moment the two corners land in one group.

Why almost O(1). Rank together with compression gives O(α(n)) amortised per operation, where α is the inverse Ackermann function, α(n) ≤ 4 for any n that fits in memory. Rank without compression is O(log n); compression without rank is also O(log n) amortised. The recursive Find above is safe precisely because of rank: the depth is at most log₂ n, which for n² = 2500 is at most 12 calls.

Exact numbers for #1631. There are at most E ≈ 2·10⁴ distinct differences. Binary search over their sorted list takes 15 checks instead of 20 and works with any values. Union-Find: 2·10⁴ edges, a sort of ≈ 3·10⁵ comparisons. Dijkstra: about 6·10⁵ on the worst map. All three fit in milliseconds; the choice is about clear code and the problem's conditions, not speed.

Unity. If the check "traversable with threshold X" is needed for many X — different characters' jump heights — Union-Find in increasing order answers them all at once: sort the thresholds, add edges, and read off an answer each time a threshold is passed.
cards/10/q: The interviewer asks about #1631: "What if the heights are fractional — float?" What do you answer?
cards/10/options/0: Dijkstra and Union-Find do not care; the binary search has to run over the sorted list of differences, or over reals with a precision
cards/10/options/1: None of the solutions works: the heights must be integers
cards/10/options/2: Only binary search on the answer works: Dijkstra needs integer weights
cards/10/explain: Dijkstra only needs a path cost that never decreases when extended; Union-Find only needs to compare edges while sorting. Binary search over integer values breaks: the answer is not between neighbouring integers. So you either search by index in the sorted list of differences, or over a real range for a fixed number of iterations.
cards/10/wrong/1: Only binary search over values needs integers. Comparing floats is perfectly fine for both a heap and a sort.
cards/10/wrong/2: The other way round: Dijkstra only needs a non-decreasing path cost, and it is binary search over values that suffers from fractions.
cards/11/q: You are solving Path With Minimum Effort out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/11/items/0: Clarify: 4 directions, the cost of a route is its largest difference, not a sum
cards/11/items/1: Name the signal: minimise the worst step — minimax
cards/11/items/2: List the solutions: Dijkstra with max, binary search + BFS, Union-Find in increasing order
cards/11/items/3: Pick Dijkstra and justify it: the cost never decreases when the path is extended
cards/11/items/4: Code: relax through max, stop when the goal is popped from the heap
cards/11/items/5: Run the example: the path 5 → 5 → 6 → 6 → 6 → 4 with effort 2
cards/11/items/6: Complexity O(E log V) and edge cases: a 1 × 1 map, all heights equal
cards/11/explain: The key is to say right away that the cost is a maximum: everything else depends on it. Three solutions with their cost show range, and the justification "the cost never decreases" shows Dijkstra was not picked at random. A 1 × 1 map gives 0: the goal is the very first cell popped.
cards/12/q: Match each solution with its cost or condition.
cards/12/pairs/1/1: O((V + E) log W), needs an integer range
cards/12/pairs/2/1: A sort in O(E log E) and almost O(1) per edge
cards/12/pairs/3/1: No sort: the heights are a permutation
cards/12/pairs/4/1: When the goal is popped, not when it gets an estimate
